## Quarto

The PHAC R User group survey results were analyzed in R through Quarto. Quarto enables you to weave together content and executable code into a finished document. Learn more about Quarto [here](https://quarto.org).

## Running Code

When you click the **Render** button a document will be generated that includes both content and the output of embedded code. 
```{r}
#The default output from Quarto is not self contained, if you want everything included in one file after you Render it, the code below will have to be in the YAML header. 

#format: 
#  html:
#    self-contained: true
```

```{r Setup, include=FALSE}
library(pacman) #installs and loads necessary packages

p_load(here,
       readxl,
       openxlsx,
       tidyverse,
       janitor, #data cleaning
       scales,
       ggtext,
       viridis,
       cowplot, #cowplot doesn't support certain fonts such as Calibri
       patchwork, 
       RColorBrewer,
       #wordcloud,
       kableExtra,
       extrafont, # so we can use the same font in the figures
       showtext,
       )

theme_survey <- function(){
  ggplot2::theme(
    # Specifies the font type and size for the entire graph
    text = element_text(family = "Calibri", size=15),         
    # the only fonts R really likes are the boring ones (Arial, Sans, etc)  
    
    # Line color for axes
    axis.line = element_line(color = 'black'),
    
    # Background of plot to clear/blank
    plot.background = element_blank(), 
    
    # Same as above for the panel
    panel.background = element_blank(), 
    
    # Removing minor grid lines
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    
    # Legend specifications
    legend.position = "bottom",                                   
    legend.title = element_blank(),                               
    legend.key = element_blank(), 
    
    # Text and background for facet_wrap titles
    strip.text = element_markdown(color = "white", size = 16),        
    strip.background = element_rect(fill="black", color="black"), 
    
    # Axis specifications
    axis.text = element_text(size=12),                           
    axis.title = element_text(size=12),                          
    axis.title.x = element_text(size=12),
    
    # NEED THIS FOR BILINGUAL TEXT element_markdown allows ggplot to read html
    axis.title.y = element_markdown(),
    #axis.title.x = element_markdown(), #if you want html in the x axis, suggest changing from element_blank() in line 64
    legend.text = element_markdown(),
    plot.title = element_markdown()
    
  )
}

# Custom color palettes
yes_no_color <- c("#CEEDDB", # honeydew
                  "#E99F9E", # salmon
                  "#8B728E") # purple-ish

three_colors <- c("#85BAA1", # Cambridge blue
                  "#5995ED", # pink
                  "#67597A") # purple

eight_colors <- c("#7768AE","#9C4D95","#FFCD29","#38C5CB","#F77271","#C1B8C8","#4D9DE0","#3BB273")

# Define 'not in'
"%!in%" <- Negate("%in%")

```
## Process Flow

```{mermaid}

flowchart LR
  A[Develop Survey] --> B(Collect responses)
  B --> C[Data cleaning]
  C --> D[Analysis]
  D --> E[Data visualization]
  C --> F(Recoding variables)
  C --> G(Formatting)
  
```
Mermaid can be used in Quarto to create process flow diagrams. 
For more information:
[Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/markdown-basics.html) and [Mermaid](https://mermaid.js.org/intro/getting-started.html).


## Import the survey data
Export the excel files from MS forms into the format of your choice. In this case we have two excel files for the survey results, one for 2023 and one for 2024.
```{r}
#| echo: false

## Clean names and add a year variable to merge all the data together

#2023 survey results
survey_2023 <- read_excel("survey_2023.xlsx")
survey_2023 <- survey_2023 %>% mutate(year=2023) %>% clean_names()

#2024 and 2025 use the same questions and format, 2023 used scales (that were not very helpful)
#2024 survey results
survey_2024 <- read_excel("survey_2024.xlsx") 
survey_2024 <- survey_2024 %>% mutate(year=2024) %>% clean_names()

#2025 survey results
survey_2025 <- read_excel("survey_2025.xlsx") 
survey_2025 <- survey_2025 %>% mutate(year=2025) %>% clean_names()
# Manually recoded "Connecting to Sharepoint; ggplot 101" to "Connecting to Sharepoint & ggplot 101"
# did not want to use any names in the code (these would have to be removed)

#merge the most recent surveys in the same format
survey_data <- bind_rows(survey_2024,survey_2025)


#min/max years
min_year <- 2023
max_year <- 2025

# Lets calculate the average survey completion time
# change the start_time and completion_time columns to a date
survey_2025$start_time <- ymd_hms(survey_2025$start_time)
survey_2025$completion_time <- ymd_hms(survey_2025$completion_time)

# Calculate time taken for each response in seconds
survey_2025$time_taken_minutes <- as.numeric(difftime(survey_2025$completion_time, survey_2025$start_time, units = "mins"))

# After a quick check, it looks like there are some outliers - maybe these were surveys that were left open
# going to exclude surveys that took over 35 mins in the average (it should have only took about 6 mins according to MS forms)
# If you want to exclude or include, you can use filter.
average_completion_time_minutes <- survey_2025 %>%
  filter(time_taken_minutes < 35) #time taken is less than 35

# Calculate average completion time in minutes
average_completion_time <- mean(average_completion_time_minutes$time_taken_minutes, na.rm = TRUE)

# round up
average_completion_round <- round(average_completion_time)

# Next, lets count the number of responses
count_2025 <- nrow(survey_2025)

# We are going to use these counts in the summary details below, using inline code. This will be displayed as an un-ordered list (<ul> <ls> list item </ls> </ul>)

```

```{r, eval=FALSE}

#How many people did we send the survey to these years?
#exported the emails from the dist list when we sent the surveys or, if that was not available, the earliest lunch and learn for the year (except the data bricks one)

files <- list.files(path = here(), pattern = "\\.txt$", full.names = TRUE)


email_counts <- sapply(files, function(file) {
  text <- read_file(file)
  email_list <- strsplit(text, ";")[[1]]
  length(trimws(email_list)) 
})


data.frame(file = basename(files), count = email_counts)

#according to google, old invites or emails with the dist-list(if it was not expanded at the time it was sent) will always export the current members in the list. So this won't work, differences here would be in the external emails.... 

```


::: {.callout-important}
Note that the results displayed are descriptive in nature. There are a number of limitations to the interpretation, however - we can use the survey results to gain some insight from those that responded.
:::

## 2025 survey results
Summary details:

* This survey was distributed in Feb `r max_year`.
* The average completion time for this survey was approximately <b> `r average_completion_round`</b> minutes^1^.
*  There were <b>`r count_2025`</b> surveys completed.

^1^ Three responses were excluded in this calculation, as they exceeded 35 minutes.

::: {.callout-note}
</b> Reminder:</b> All surveys cover the evaluation of the PHAC R Usergroup for the previous year (e.g. The 2025 survey evaluates activities in 2024).
:::

### 1) When did you join the PHAC R User group?
```{r}
#| echo: false

# For the ease of learning for beginners, the data analysis and visualization will be completed in a way that is hopefully easy to understand/follow - can be adjusted to me more efficient. I'm taking each column and isolating it in a separate data frame.

#to list all the variables in your dataframe, remove the # in the next line (un-comment)
# ls(survey_2025)

# once you decide which columnns you want to keep, you can use select
when_joined <- survey_2025 %>%
  select(id,when_did_you_join_the_phac_r_user_group)

# Next we can summarize our data - you can also complete this in the last step using a pipe (%>%)

when_joined2 <- when_joined %>%
  group_by(when_did_you_join_the_phac_r_user_group) %>% # group the responses in this column to count
  summarise(n=n()) %>% # creates the count
  mutate(denom = sum(n, na.rm=T)) %>% # create the denominator
  mutate(proportion = round_half_up(n/denom*100,1))


fig1 <- when_joined2 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_relevel(when_did_you_join_the_phac_r_user_group, 
                             "before 2023",
                             "2023",
                             "2024",
                             "2025"),
             y = proportion, 
             label = proportion)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge", fill = c("#7768AE","#9C4D95","#FFCD29","#38C5CB")) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0,0.2))) +
 # scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis", guide = "none") + #if you want to use viridis
  geom_text(size = 4, vjust = -0.5, family = "Calibri") +
  labs(x = "Responses",
       y = "Percent (%)") +
  #ggtitle(paste("Question 1) When did you join the PHAC R User group", max_year)) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12)) +
  theme(plot.caption = element_text(hjust=0)) +
  theme_survey() 

fig1

```

### 2) Which presentations did you attend (in the past 12 months)?
Select all that apply.
```{r, out.width="100%", out.height="auto", dpi=300, fig.align='right'}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

which_presentations <- survey_2025 %>%
  select(id,which_presentations_did_you_attend_over_the_past_12_months_select_all_that_apply)

# This column needs some cleaning, since it was a select all that apply question, we have a list in the responses. We need to parse these out! For simplicity, I'm going to separate them by ; and keep the presentation titles

# Create a new variable by splitting the values into separate columns
which_presentations2 <- which_presentations %>%
  separate(which_presentations_did_you_attend_over_the_past_12_months_select_all_that_apply, 
           into = paste0("col", 1:12), sep = ";")

# Remove the cols that have the presenters
which_presentations3 <- which_presentations2 %>%
  select(id,col1,col3,col5,col7,col9,col11)


# Pivot the data longer
long_which_presentations <- which_presentations3 %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("col"), 
               names_to = "column", 
               values_to = "responses") #changing the column name 

# select the columns, remove NAs & blank cells, and summarise the data!
long_which_presentations1 <- long_which_presentations %>%
  select(id,responses) %>%
  filter(!is.na(responses) & responses != "") 

long_which_presentations2 <- long_which_presentations1 %>%
  group_by(responses) %>% # group the responses in this column to count
  summarise(n=n()) %>% # creates the count
  mutate(denom = sum(n, na.rm=T)) %>% # create the denominator
  mutate(proportion = round_half_up(n/denom*100,1))

long_which_presentations2$responses <- factor(long_which_presentations2$responses, 
     levels = long_which_presentations2$responses[order(-long_which_presentations2$proportion)])


fig2 <- long_which_presentations2 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = proportion,
             y = fct_relevel(responses, 
                             "Version control using Github",
                             "Intro to report building",
                             "Using Python, Javascript and R in Quarto for Data Analysis",
                             "Report building",
                             "Forecasting in R",
                             "Implementing differential privacy in R",
                             "None"),
             label = proportion)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge", fill = "#D0E3C4") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0,0.2))) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis", guide = "none") +
  geom_text(size = 4, vjust = -0.5, family="Calibri") +
  labs(x = "Percent (%)",
       y = NA) +
 # ggtitle(paste("Question 2) Which presentations did you attend", max_year)) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12)) +
  theme(plot.caption = element_text(hjust=0)) +
  theme_survey() 

fig2

```

### 6) What is preventing you from using R more often? 
Select all that apply
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

# this also needs to be cleaned up!
preventing_r <- survey_2025 %>%
  select(id,what_is_preventing_you_from_using_r_more_often_select_all_that_apply) %>%
  separate(what_is_preventing_you_from_using_r_more_often_select_all_that_apply, 
           into = paste0("col", 1:3), sep = ";")

# Pivot the data longer
long_preventing_r  <- preventing_r %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("col"), 
               names_to = "column", 
               values_to = "responses") #changing the column name 

# select the columns, remove NAs & blank cells, and summarise the data!
long_preventing_r1 <- long_preventing_r  %>%
  select(id,responses) %>%
  filter(!is.na(responses) & responses != "") 

# This question had a number of other responses, need to recode
#look at the responses that are in the questionnaire, recode the rest to Other

#unique(long_preventing_r1$responses) #can use to check the unique responses

#here I am creating a list of the responses in the question
response_options <- c("Installing and updating software (R, RStudio, and packages)",
                      "Steep learning curve",
                      "Lack of management support",
                      "Lack of technical support",
                      "Not applicable - I am using R an adequate amount")

long_preventing_r2 <- long_preventing_r1 %>%
  mutate(responses2 = case_when(responses %!in% response_options ~"Other",
                               T ~ responses))
# one could do additional cleaning here but I'm leaving this as is 


long_preventing_r3 <- long_preventing_r2 %>%
  group_by(responses2) %>% # group the responses in this column to count
  summarise(n=n()) %>% # creates the count
  mutate(denom = sum(n, na.rm=T)) %>% # create the denominator
  mutate(proportion = round_half_up(n/denom*100,1))

# 
fig6 <- long_preventing_r3 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = proportion,
             y = fct_relevel(responses2, 
                             "Other",
                             "Not applicable - I am using R an adequate amount",
                             "Steep learning curve",
                             "Lack of technical support",
                             "Installing and updating software (R, RStudio, and packages)",
                             "Lack of management support"),
             label = proportion)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge", fill = "#D0E3C4") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0,0.2))) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis", guide = "none") +
  geom_text(size = 4, vjust = -0.5, family="Calibri") +
  labs(x = "Proportion (%)",
       y = "Responses") +
 # ggtitle(paste("Question 2) Which presentations did you attend", max_year)) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12)) +
  theme(plot.caption = element_text(hjust=0)) +
  theme_survey() 

fig6

#Lets also look at the Other responses
other_preventing_r <- long_preventing_r2 %>%
  filter(responses2 == "Other") %>%
  select(responses) %>%
  rename("Other responses" = responses)

kable(other_preventing_r, format = "html") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

```

```{r}
                             "Python",
                             "None",

  geom_point(size = 4, color = "#D0E3C4", fill = "white") +  # Change color and size as desired
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0,0.2))) +
  labs(x = "Proportion (%)",

  geom_text(size = 4, vjust = -0.5, family="Calibri") +
```

### 9) Would you be interested in learning Python^1^ in this user group? 

^1^Python is a programming language that is commonly used in the data community. 
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

# The name of this var is too long, renaming
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

#2023 survey
survey_2023 <- survey_2023 %>%
  clean_names()

#Survey completion time
survey_2023$start_time <- ymd_hms(survey_2023$start_time)
survey_2023$completion_time <- ymd_hms(survey_2023$completion_time)

# Calculate time taken for each response in seconds
survey_2023$time_taken_minutes <- as.numeric(difftime(survey_2023$completion_time, survey_2023$start_time, units = "mins"))

# If you want to exclude or include, you can use filter.
average_completion_time_minutes_2023 <- survey_2023 %>%
  filter(time_taken_minutes < 35) #time taken is less than 35

# Calculate average completion time in minutes
average_completion_time_2023 <- mean(average_completion_time_minutes_2023$time_taken_minutes, na.rm = TRUE)

# round up
average_completion_round_2023 <- round(average_completion_time_2023)

# Next, lets count the number of responses
count_2023 <- nrow(survey_2023)

```

# Comparing results to other years

## `r min_year` survey results
Summary details:

* This survey was distributed in May `r min_year`.
* The average completion time for this survey was approximately <b> `r average_completion_round_2023`</b> minutes^1^.
*  There were <b>`r count_2023`</b> surveys completed.

^1^ Four responses were excluded in this calculation, as they exceeded 35 minutes.

::: {.callout-note}
Note that only select questions are shown for the 2023 survey. Questions that had a scale are not included.
:::

```{r}
long_mentoring3_2023 <- long_mentoring2_2023 %>%
  group_by(responses2) %>% # group the responses in this column to count
  summarise(n=n()) %>% # creates the count
  mutate(denom = sum(n, na.rm=T)) %>% # create the denominator
  mutate(proportion = round_half_up(n/denom*100,1))

# lets make this a lollipop plot
fig_m <- long_mentoring3_2023  %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = proportion,
             y = fct_relevel(responses2, 
                      "MS Teams Q&A Space",
                      "Drop-in office hours",
                      "One-on-one sessions",
                      "On-call help",
                      "Not interested",
                      "Other"),
             label = proportion)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = 0, yend = fct_relevel(responses2, 
                      "MS Teams Q&A Space",
                      "Drop-in office hours",
                      "One-on-one sessions",
                      "On-call help",
                      "Not interested",
                      "Other")),
               color = "black") +  # Change color as desired
  geom_point(size = 4, color = "#8B728E", fill = "white") +  # Change color and size as desired
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0,0.2))) +
  labs(x = "Proportion (%)",
       y = "Responses") +
  geom_text(size = 4, vjust = -0.5, family="Calibri") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12)) +
  theme(plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0)) +
  theme_survey()

fig_m

#Lets also look at the Other responses
other_mentoring_2023 <- long_mentoring2_2023 %>%
  filter(responses2 == "Other") %>%
  select(responses)%>%
  rename("Other responses" = responses)

kable(other_mentoring_2023, format = "html") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

```

## 2022 survey results
Summary details:

* This survey was distributed in November 2020-January 2021.
* It was distributed using Google forms.
* There were <b> 16 </b> surveys completed.

## 2021 survey results
Summary details:

* This survey was distributed in November 2021-January 2022.
  * this was a housekeeping survey following the pandemic
* It was distributed using Google forms.
* There were <b> 27 </b> surveys completed.



::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
<b>Limitations include: </b>poor response rate, non-standardized questionnaires, the second survey was anonymous (we can't compare directly between years based on participants), may not be representative of the community as a whole, subject to bias etc.
:::
